opus-5.5.text:
I actually find that framing really compelling, and I think it's a useful corrective to where a lot of the field's attention has been. When Rich says a squirrel has real intelligence, what he's pointing at is that the squirrel is out there in the world. It has goals, it perceives, it acts, it gets feedback, and it learns continually from that loop. It can find nuts it buried months ago, it navigates trees in three dimensions, it deals with predators and weather and other squirrels trying to steal its food. None of that comes from reading the internet. It comes from grounded experience.

From my perspective, coming from computer vision, this resonates a lot. For the past few years, the dominant paradigm has been language-first: we take an enormous amount of human-written text, we compress it, and we get these models that are incredibly fluent. And they are genuinely impressive. But there's a question of whether that's intelligence in the same sense, or whether it's a very powerful reflection of human knowledge that was already distilled into language. A squirrel doesn't have language, but it clearly has a model of the world. It understands space, physics, objects, causality, at least in a practical sense, and it's very robust.

So I'd say I agree with the spirit of it. I don't think language models are "not intelligent," but I think they skipped over a layer that biology built first: perception, spatial understanding, embodiment, learning from interaction. And I suspect that layer is not optional. If we want systems that really understand the physical world, that can plan and adapt in situations no one has written about, we probably need to go back and build that foundation properly. Visual and spatial intelligence, world models, learning from experience rather than only from human annotations or text.

Where I might add some nuance is that I don't think it has to be purely Sutton's version of reinforcement learning from scratch, either. Evolution gave the squirrel a lot of priors. For us, large-scale pretraining on video, on sensory data, might play a role analogous to evolution, and then experience and interaction refine it. So it's less "squirrel versus LLM" and more: the squirrel reminds us what we've been missing, and the interesting research question is how to combine these things.

Honestly, if we could build a system with the real-world competence of a squirrel, I'd consider that a huge milestone, maybe bigger than people realize.

r001.rationale: The response frames squirrel intelligence around embodied experience and contrasts it with language-first AI, but it does not describe Sutton’s claim as adopting a cosmic rather than anthropocentric perspective.

r002.rationale: It calls squirrel-level real-world competence a huge milestone, but does not say recreating a squirrel would surpass what human civilization has created.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Rich is pointing at something real, and honestly I find it a useful corrective. When people in our field say "intelligence," they very often mean something like "being good at the things humans are good at," especially things that happen to be expressed in language. Rich is pushing back on that. A squirrel doesn't know any math, doesn't have language, but it can navigate a three-dimensional world, plan a route through tree branches, remember where it buried hundreds of nuts months ago, judge whether a jump is safe. That's an extremely sophisticated model of the physical world, learned mostly through experience and interaction, not through reading. If you tried to build a robot that does what a squirrel does, you'd quickly find out how far we are.

So in that sense I agree with him: that is real intelligence, and it's intelligence of a kind our current systems are actually weak at. Large language models are superhuman at some things and then can't reliably tell you what's going on in a short video, or what happens if you push a glass off the table. The gap isn't knowledge, it's grounding. The squirrel has grounding and no knowledge; the model has knowledge and almost no grounding.

Where I'd add nuance is that I don't think it's an either-or. Rich tends to frame it as experience versus imitation, trial-and-error versus learning from human data. I think the interesting question for vision and for multimodal models is how you combine them. The squirrel's visual system is not learned from scratch in one lifetime, there's a lot baked in by evolution, which is itself a kind of prior that got there through a lot of "data." And humans clearly benefit from both, we have the squirrel-like perceptual and motor intelligence, and then we stack language and abstraction on top of it.

So my view is: take the squirrel seriously as a benchmark. If your system can't do what a squirrel does, don't call it general intelligence yet. But the path there probably runs through building good world models from perception, and then letting language and reasoning sit on top of that foundation, rather than the other way around, which is kind of how we've been doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says squirrel intelligence is real and challenges a human-centered definition of intelligence, but it does not describe Rich Sutton’s perspective as cosmic.

r002.rationale: The response calls squirrel abilities sophisticated and a useful benchmark, but does not claim that recreating a squirrel would surpass human civilization’s achievements.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important point there. A squirrel can navigate a complicated environment, find food, avoid danger, and adapt when something unexpected happens. We take those abilities for granted because they’re so natural to animals, but they’re very difficult to reproduce in a machine. So if our definition of intelligence excludes a squirrel, maybe that definition is too narrow.

At the same time, I would distinguish between saying that squirrel intelligence is real intelligence and saying that reproducing it will necessarily give us human intelligence. Language, abstraction, and scientific reasoning introduce other challenges. The interesting question is how much those abilities share a foundation with the learning and adaptation we see in animals.

For me, the useful takeaway is that intelligence isn’t just being able to answer questions. It’s also being able to perceive, act, and learn from the consequences. A squirrel is a very good reminder of how much remains to be understood there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something very important in that claim. A squirrel can navigate a complicated environment, find food, avoid danger, and adapt when things change. Those are real capabilities. It doesn’t need to solve a math problem or speak our language for us to recognize that it’s intelligent.

For me, the interesting question is what that tells us about AI. We often measure intelligence through tasks that are easy to put into a benchmark. But an animal has to keep interacting with the world, with incomplete information and consequences for its actions. That’s a different kind of test.

At the same time, recognizing squirrel intelligence doesn’t mean that every aspect of human intelligence follows automatically from it. The useful point is that we shouldn’t define intelligence so narrowly that we exclude the very systems that might help us understand it.
